1Middle-α Cantor Sets

Let α∈(0,1), and let Cα​ be the middle-α Cantor set.

Goal. Construct Cα,n​, which is a union of 2n disjoint closed intervals, indexed by i=i1​,i2​,…,in​∈{0,1}n, each of length (21−α​)n, such that Cα​=⋂n=0∞​Cα,n​.

例 1.1. Classical Cantor set α=31​, I=[0,1]. C31​,0​C31​,1​C31​,2​(Index⋯C31​,n​Cα,n​​:=I:=[0,31​]∪[32​,1]:=[0,91​]∪[92​,31​]∪[32​,97​]∪[98​,1]:32​⋅0+92​⋅0,32​⋅0+92​⋅1,32​⋅1+92​⋅0,32​⋅1+92​⋅1 indicate where these intervals begin):=i1​,i2​,…,in​∈{0,1}⋃​[k=1∑n​3k2​ik​,k=1∑n​3k2​ik​+(31​)n]:=i∈{0,1}n⋃​Ii​.​

By removing from Ii​ the open interval with the same center as Ii​ and length α∣Ii​∣, we obtain two subintervals Ii1​i2​⋯in​0​ and Ii1​i2​⋯in​1​. Cα,n+1​​:=i∈{0,1}n⋃​(Ii0​∪Ii1​)=i∈{0,1}n+1⋃​Ii​.​Clearly, Cα,n+1​⊂Cα,n​, and ∀k,Cα,k​ is compact. Thus Cα​=⋂n=0∞​Cα,n​ is compact and non-empty.

注 1.2.

(i)

L1(Cα​)=0,∀α∈(0,1);

(ii)

Cα​ are mutually homeomorphic.

From the remark above we know that the Lebesgue measure is not a good tool to measure the size of Cantor sets. We will introduce Minkovski dimension to study the size of Cα​.

2Minkovski Dimension

By talking about dimension, we want to know how a set scales. For example, a line segment of length L can be covered by ϵL​ intervals of length ϵ. A square of side length L can be covered by (ϵL​)2 squares of side length ϵ. A cube of side length L can be covered by (ϵL​)3 cubes of side length ϵ. Thus we have the following definition.

定义 2.1.

(i)

∀E⊂Rn, the diameter of E is defined as diamE:=supx,y∈E​∣x−y∣.

(ii)

If E⊂⋃α∈A​Eα​ then {Eα​}α∈A​ is a covering of E. If {Eα​}α∈A​ also satisfies diamEα​≤δ,∀α∈A, then it is called a δ-covering of E.

定义 2.2.

(i)

Given a bounded set K⊂Rn, let N(K,δ) be the minimal cardinality of a δ-covering of K, i.e., N(K,δ)=min{J:K⊂⋃j=1J​Ej​,dim(Ej​)≤δ}.

(ii)

The upper Minkovski dimension of a bounded set K is dimM​(K):=δ→0limsup​−logδlogN(K,δ)​.The lower Minkovski dimension of a bounded set K is dim​M​(K):=δ→0liminf​−logδlogN(K,δ)​.

(iii)

If dimM​(K)=dim​M​(K), then we call it the Minkovski dimension of K, denoted by dimM​(K).

注 2.3.

(i)

dimM​(K)=α iff ∀ϵ>0,∃δ0​>0, s.t. δ−α−ϵ≤N(K,δ)≤δ−α+ϵ,∀δ∈(0,δ0​).

(ii)

dim​M​(K)=α iff ∀ϵ>0,∃δ0​>0, s.t. −α−ϵ≤η∈(0,δ)inf​logη−1logN(K,η)​≤−α+ϵ,∀δ∈(0,δ0​).

(iii)

E⊂F⇔dimM​E≤dimM​F.

引理 2.4.

(i)

Let NB​(K,δ) be the minimal cardinality of a covering of E consisting of balls of radius δ. Then dimM​(K)=limδ→0​−logδlogNB​(K,δ)​ whenever dimM​(K) exists.

(ii)

In (i), it is equivalent to use axis-aligned cubes of side length δ to cover K.

(iii)

If A⊂Rn is bounded, then dimM​(A)=dimM​(Aˉ), dim​M​(A)=dim​M​(Aˉ).

证明. (i) Let NB​(K,δ) be the minimal cardinality of a covering of E consisting of balls of radius δ. Then any such covering is also a δ-covering, so N(K,δ)≤NB​(K,δ). On the other hand, if {Ej​}j=1N(K,δ)​ is a δ-covering of K, then {B(xj​,δ)}j=1N(K,δ)​ is a covering of K, where xj​∈Ej​. Thus NB​(K,δ)≤N(K,δ). Hence N(K,δ)=NB​(K,δ), and the result follows.

(ii) Similar to (i).

(iii) We fix a covering {Ej​}j=1J​ of A with Bj​=B(aj​,δ) satisfying J=NB​(A,δ). As J is finite, we have Aj​ˉ​⊆j=1⋃J​Bj​​=j=1⋃J​Bj​​=j=1⋃J​Bj​.□

例 2.5.

(i)

If E is finite, then dimM​(E)=0.

(ii)

If E is a line segment in Rn, then dimM​(E)=1. More generally, any compact k-dimensional C1 submanifold of Rn has Minkovski dimension k.

(iii)

Let 0<α<1, then dimM​(Cα​)=log2−log(1−α)log2​.

(iv)

If E⊆Rn and dimM​E<n, then Ln(E)=0.

(v)

Let E={0}∪{1,21​,31​,…}, then dimM​E=21​.

(Idea: cover the first n points from 1, then cover the rest points from n1​ by n intervals of length n21​.)

注 2.6. From (v) we know that Minkovski dimension is not countably stable, i.e., dimM​(⋃i=1∞​Ei​)=supi​dimM​(Ei​) in general.

For a given set E⊂Rn, we define the δ-neighborhood of E as Eδ​:={y∈Rn:dist(y,E)<δ}.

引理 2.7. Let α>0, suppose that ∃Aα​>0 s.t. L(Eδ​)≥Aα​δα, ∀δ>0. Then dim​M​(E)≥n−α.

证明. Suppose E⊆⋃j=1J​B(xj​,δ), then Eδ​⊆⋃j=1J​B(xj​,2δ), which implies that Aα​δα≤L(Eδ​)≤Cn​Jδn. As a result, NB​(E,δ)≥Aα,n​δ−(n−α). Therefore dim​M​(E)≥n−α.

□

3Measures

Let X be a non-empty set. Denote by 2X be the power set of X, i.e., the set of all subsets of X.

定义 3.1. A map μ:2X→[0,+∞] is called a measure on X if

(i)

μ(∅)=0;

(ii)

(Countable subadditivity) If A⊆⋃k=1∞​Ak​, then μ(A)≤∑k=1∞​μ(Ak​).

注 3.2. In most references, the measure as defined above is called an outer measure.

定义 3.3. Let μ be a measure on X. C is a subset of X. Define the restriction of μ to C as μ∣C​(A):=μ(A∩C),∀A⊆X.

定义 3.4. A set A⊆X is called μ-measurable if ∀B⊆X, μ(B)=μ(B∩A)+μ(B∩Ac).

定理 3.5. Let μ be a measure on X.

(i)

If A⊆B⊆X, then μ(A)≤μ(B)≤μ(X).

(ii)

If A⊆X is μ-measurable, then so is Ac.

(iii)

∅ and X are μ-measurable. Moreover, if μ(A)=0, then A is μ-measurable.

(iv)

Let C⊆X. Then any μ-measurable set is also μ∣C​-measurable.

证明.

(ii)

μ(B)=μ(B∩A)+μ(B∖A)=μ(B∖AC)+μ(B∩AC).

(iv)

μ∣C​(B)=μ(B∩C)=μ((B∩C)∩A)+μ((B∩C)∩Ac)=μ∣C​(B∩A)+μ∣C​(B∩Ac).

□

定理 3.6. Let {Ak​}k=1∞​ be a sequence of μ-measurable sets.

(i)

If Ak​ are pairwise disjoint, then μ(⋃k=1∞​Ak​)=∑k=1∞​μ(Ak​).

(ii)

If A1​⊆⋯⊆Ak​⊆Ak+1​⊆⋯, then k→∞lim​μ(Ak​)=μ(k=1⋃∞​Ak​).

(iii)

If A1​⊇⋯⊇Ak​⊇Ak+1​⊇⋯ and μ(A1​)<+∞, then k→∞lim​μ(Ak​)=μ(k=1⋂∞​Ak​).

(iv)

⋃k=1∞​Ak​ and ⋂k=1∞​Ak​ are μ-measurable.

证明. First we prove that for finie n, ⋃k=1n​Ak​ is measurable. By induction, we only need to prove the case n=2. For any B⊆X, μ(B)​=μ(B∩A1​)+μ(B∩A1C​)=μ(B∩A1​)+μ(B∩A1C​∩A2​)+μ(B∩A1C​∩A2C​)≥μ(B∩(A1​∪A2​))+μ(B∩(A1​∪A2​)C).​(Note that A1​∪A2​=A1​∪(A1C​∩A2​).) Thus A1​∪A2​ is measurable. Now (A1​∩A2​)C=A1C​∪A2C​, so A1​∩A2​ is also measurable.

(i)

Let Bj​=⋃k=1j​Ak​. Then μ(Bj+1​)​=μ(Bj+1​∩Aj+1​)+μ(Bj+1​∩Aj+1C​)=μ(Aj+1​)+μ(Bj​),​therefore μ(⋃k=1∞​Ak​)≥μ(⋃k=1j​Ak​)=∑k=1j​μ(Ak​). By letting j→∞, we obtain the result from subadditivity.

(ii)

From (i) we know k→∞lim​μ(Ak​)​=μ(A1​)+k=1∑∞​(μ(Ak+1​)−μ(Ak​))=μ(A1​)+k=1∑∞​μ(Ak+1​∖Ak​)=μ(k=1⋃∞​Ak​).​

(iii)

Let Bk​=A1​∖Ak​, then by (ii) we have k→∞lim​​μ(Bk​)=μ(k=1⋃∞​Bk​)=μ(A1​∖k=1⋂∞​Ak​)⟺μ(A1​)<+∞​k→∞lim​μ(Ak​)=μ(k=1⋂∞​Ak​).​

(iv)

Since Bj​=⋃k=1j​Ak​ is measurable, for any B⊆X with μ(B)<∞, we have μ(B∩k=1⋃∞​Ak​)+μ(B∖k=1⋃∞​Ak​)​=μ∣B​(k=1⋃∞​Ak​)+μ∣B​(k=1⋂∞​Ak​)=k→∞lim​[μ∣B​(Bk​)+μ∣B​(BkC​)]=μ(B).​That is, ⋃k=1∞​Ak​ is μ-measurable. (⋂k=1∞​Ak​)C=⋃k=1∞​AkC​⇒⋂k=1∞​Ak​ is also μ-measurable.

□

定义 3.7. A collection of subsets A⊂2X is called a σ-algebra if

(i)

∅,X∈A;

(ii)

A∈A⇒Ac:=X∖A∈A;

(iii)

Ak​∈A,k∈Z+​⇒⋃k=1∞​Ak​∈A.

注 3.8. ⋂k=1∞​Ak​=(⋃k=1∞​Akc​)c∈A.

定理 3.9. Let μ be a measure on a nonempty set X. Then the collection M of all μ-measurable subsets of X is a σ-algebra.

注 3.10. By Theorem 3.6(i), μ is countably additive on M.

定义 3.11. If C⊂2X is a nonempty collection of subsets of X, the σ-algebra generated by C, denoted by σ(C), is the smallest σ-algebra containing C.

注 3.12. σ(C) is the intersection of all σ-algebra containing C.

定义 3.13.

(i)

The Borel σ-algebra of Rn is the smallest σ-algebra B of Rn containing all open subsets of Rn. An element in B is called a Borel set.

(ii)

A measure μ is called Borel if every Borel set is μ-measurable.

定理 3.14 (Caratheodory’s criterion). Let μ be a measure on Rn. If for all sets A,B⊂Rn, we have μ(A∪B)=μ(A)+μ(B)whenever dist(A,B)>0(1)then μ is a Borel measure.

证明. It suffices to show that a closed set C is μ-measurable, which follows from the inequality μ(A)≥μ(A∩C)+μ(A∖C),∀A⊂Rn.(2)We may assume μ(A)<∞, or otherwise (2) is trivial.

Define for all n∈Z+​ Cn​:={x∈Rn:dist(x,C)≤n1​},then dist(A∩C,A∩Cnc​)≥n1​>0.

By (1), μ(A∩C)+μ(A∩Cnc​)=μ((A∩C)∪(A∩Cnc​)),we complete the proof if we have n→∞lim​μ(A∩Cnc​)=μ(A∩Cc).(3)For k∈Z+​, define Rk​:={x∈A:(k+1)−1<dist(x,C)≤k−1}.Observe that dist(Ri​,Rj​)>0 if j≥i+2, therefore, by (1), k=1∑j​μ(R2k​)=μ(k=1⋃j​R2k​)≤μ(A).Taking j→∞, and considering the odd terms, we have k=1∑∞​μ(Rk​)≤2μ(A)<∞.In particular, n→∞lim​k=n∑∞​μ(Rk​)=0.Recalling that C is closed, dist(x,C)>0,∀x∈Cc, which implies that A∩Cc=(A∩Cnc​)∪(k=n⋃∞​Rk​).As a result, μ(A∩Cnc​)≤μ(A∩C)≤μ(A∩Cnc​)+k=n∑∞​μ(Rk​).Taking n→∞, we obtain (3).

□

Radon Measures

定义 3.15. Let μ be a measure on X.

(i)

μ is locally finite if ∀x∈X,∃r>0 s.t. μ(B(x,r))<∞.

(ii)

μ is Borel regular if it is a Borel measure and ∀A⊂X,∃ a Borel set B⊂X s.t. A⊂B, and μ(A)=μ(B).

(iii)

μ is a Radon measure if it is Borel regular and locally finite.

注 3.16.

(i)

On Rn, μ is locally finite iff μ(K)<∞ for all compact K.

(ii)

The initial definition of measure does not relate to topology, but Radon measures do.

定理 3.17. Let μ be a Borel regular measure on Rn. Suppose A⊂Rn is μ-measurable and μ(A)<∞. Then μ∣A​ is a Radon measure.

注 3.18. If A is a Borel set, then μ∣A​ is Borel regular even if μ(A)=∞.

证明. Denote ν:=μ∣A​. Obviously, ν(K)<∞ for all compact K. As every μ-measurable set is ν-measurable, and μ is Borel, we have that ν is Borel.

It remains to show that ∀C⊂Rn,∃ a Borel set B⊃C s.t. ν(B)=ν(C).

We may assume that A is a Borel set. In fact, ∃ a Borel set B s.t. A⊂B and μ(A)=μ(B) as μ is regular. Which implies that μ∣B​(C)​=μ(B∩C∩A)+μ(B∩C∩Ac)≤μ(A∩C)+μ(B∩Ac)=μ(A∩C)+μ(B)−μ(A)=μ∣A​(C)​as A is measurable, and μ(A)<∞.

Fix C⊂Rn, then ∃ a Borel set E s.t. A∩C⊂E, and μ(A∩C)=μ(E). Let D:=E∪Ac, which is Borel. Then C⊂(A∩C)∪Ac⊂D, and ν(D)=μ(D∩A)≤μ(E∩A)≤μ(E)=ν(C). Hence ν(C)=ν(D).

□

注 3.19. Hausdorff measure is infinite on lower dimensional subspaces. But Radon measure requires a finite value on compact sets. Therefore, most Hausdorff measures are not Radon measures.

引理 3.20. Let μ be a Borel measure on Rn, and let B be a Borel set.

(i)

If μ(B)<∞, then ∀ϵ>0,∃ a closed set C s.t. C⊂B and μ(B∖C)<ϵ.

(ii)

If μ is a Radon measure, then ∀ϵ>0, ∃ an open set U s.t. B⊂U, and μ(U∖B)<ϵ.

证明. Let ν:=μ∣B​, which is a finite Borel measure. Let F:={A⊂Rn:A is μ-measurable, and ∀ϵ>0,∃ closed C s.t. ν(A∖C)<ϵ}.Obviously, all closed sets are in F. We will show that G:={A∈F:Rn∖A∈F}is a σ-algebra containing all Borel sets. In particular, B∈G, i.e., (i) holds.

Claim 1 If {Ai​}i=1∞​⊂F, then A=⋂i=1∞​Ai​∈F

Proof of Claim 1: Fix ϵ>0. Since Ai​∈F, ∃ a closed set Ci​⊂Ai​ s.t. ν(Ai​∖Ci​)<2−i−1ϵ. Let C=⋂i=1∞​Ci​, then C is closed, and ν(A∖C)≤ν(i=1⋃∞​(Cic​∩Ai​))<ϵ.

Claim 2 If {Ai​}i=1∞​⊂F, then A:=⋃i=1∞​Ai​⊂F.

Proof of Claim 2: As ν(A)<∞, we have m→∞lim​ν(A∖i=1⋃m​Ci​)≤ν(i=1⋃∞​(Ai​∩Cic​))<2ϵ​.Consequently, ∃m s.t. μ(A∖⋃i=1m​Ci​)<ϵ, as ⋃i=1m​Ci​ is closed, A∈F.

As every open set in Rn can be written as a countable union of closed sets, we obtain from Claim 2 that F contains all open sets. By definition, G contains all open sets. Suppose {Ai​}i=1∞​⊂G, then Ai​,Aic​∈F. By Claim 1 and 2, ⋃i=1∞​Ai​,⋂i=1∞​Aic​∈F, hence ⋃i=1∞​Ai​∈G. As a result, G is a σ-algebra containing all Borel sets.

For (ii): Let Um​:=B(0,m)={x∈Rn:∣x∣≤m}. As μ is Radon, we have μ(Um​∖B)<∞. Applying (i), we find a closed set Cm​⊂Um​∩Bc s.t. μ(Um​∩Bc∩Cmc​)<2−mϵ. Let U:=⋃m=1∞​(Um​∪Cmc​), which is open. As Cm​⊂Bc, we have B⊂Cmc​, and therefore Um​∩B⊂Um​∩Cmc​. Consequently, B⊂U. Furthermore, μ(U∖B)≤∑m​μ(Um​∩Cmc​∩Bc)<ϵ.

□

定理 3.21. Let μ be a Radon measure on Rn. Then

(i)

∀A⊂Rn, μ(A)=inf{μ(U):A⊂U,U is open}(4)(inner regularity)

(ii)

∀μ-measurable set A⊂Rn, μ(A)=sup{μ(K):K⊂A,K is compact}(outer regularity)

注 3.22. In many references this is taken as the definition of Radon measure, but geometric measure theory often uses the definition above.

证明. The conclusion is obvious if μ(A)=∞, so we assume μ(A)<∞.

Suppose A is Borel. Fixing ϵ>0, by Lemma above, ∃ an open set U⊃A s.t. μ(U∖A)<ϵ. As A is μ-measurable, we have μ(U)=μ(A)+μ(U∩Ac), which implies (4).

For an arbitrary set A, ∃ a Borel set B s.t. A⊂B and μ(A)=μ(B). Then μ(A)=μ(B)=inf{μ(U):B⊂U,U is open}≥inf{μ(U):A⊂U,U is open}.The opposite inequality is trivial, so (i) holds.

For (ii): Consider first the case μ(A)<∞. Let ν:=μ∣A​, which is Radon by previous theorem. Fixing ϵ>0, and applying (i) to ν and Ac, ∃ an open set U⊃Ac s.t. ν(U)≤ϵ. Denote C=Uc, then C is closed, and C⊂A. Moreover, μ(A∖C)=ν(Cc)≤ϵ. Thus, 0≤μ(A)−μ(C)≤ϵ, and therefore μ(A)=sup{μ(C):C⊂A,C is closed}.

Let Cm​:=C∩B(0,m)​, then Cm​ is compact, and limm→∞​μ(Cm​)=μ(C). Then (ii) holds when μ(A)<∞.

Now suppose μ(A)=∞. Define Dk​:={x∈Rn:k−1≤∣x∣<k}. Then A=⋃k=1∞​(Dk​∩A), which implies that ∞=μ(A)=∑k=1∞​μ(Dk​∩A). Since μ is Radon, μ(Dk​∩A)<∞. Then ∃ a compact set Ck​⊂Dk​∩A s.t. μ(Ck​)≥μ(Dk​∩A)−2−k−1. As a result, ⋃k=1∞​Ck​⊂A, limm→∞​(⋃k=1∞​Ck​)=μ(⋃k=1∞​Ck​)=∑μ(Ck​)=∞. This yields (ii) as ⋃k=1m​Ck​ is compact.

□

定义 3.23.

(i)

A topological space X is called locally compact if every point has a compact neighborhood.

(ii)

X is called σ-compact if it is a countable union of compact sets.

定理 3.24. Let X be a locally compact Hausdorff space in which every open set is σ-compact. Then every Borel measure on X that is finite on compact sets is Radon. (Proof omitted.)

4Hausdorff Measures and Hausdorff Dimensions

Hausdorff Measures

定义 4.1.

(i)

Let A⊂Rn, 0≤s<∞, 0<δ≤∞. Define Hδs​(A):=inf{j=1∑∞​α(s)(2diamCj​​)s:A⊂j=1⋃∞​Cj​,diamCj​≤δ},where α(s):=Γ(2s​+1)πs/2​.

(ii)

定义Hs(A):=δ→0lim​Hδs​(A)=δ>0sup​Hδs​(A).

注 4.2. α(s) 是一个与球体积有关的常数, 是为了使 s 取整时 Hausdorff 测度与经典 Lebesgue 测度相等. 其并不会对 Hausdorff 维数产生本性影响.

注 4.3.

(i)

Γ(s):=∫0∞​e−xxs−1dx.

(ii)

α(n)=Ln(B(0,1)).

(iii)

Hn=Ln.

(iv)

The definition remains equivalent if we assume that Cj​ are closed balls.

定义 4.4.

(i)

Let A⊂Rn, 0≤s<∞, 0<δ≤∞. Define Hδs​(A):=inf{i=1∑∞​α(s)(2diamCj​​)s:A⊂j=1⋃∞​Cj​,diamCj​≤δ},where α(s) is as above.

(ii)

Define Hs(A):=δ→0lim​Hδs​(A)=δ>0sup​Hδs​(A).

定理 4.5. For all 0≤s<n, Hs is a Borel regular measure in Rn.

证明. Step 1 Hδs​ is a measure. Clearly Hδs​=0. Suppose A⊂⋃j=1∞​Aj​. Take a δ-covering {Cjk​}k=1∞​ of Aj​ for each j, then {Cjk​}j,k=1,2,…​ is a δ-covering of A. This implies Hδs​(A)≤j=1∑∞​k=1∑∞​(diamCjk​)sTaking the infimum, we get Hδs​(A)≤j=1∑∞​Hδs​(Aj​).(5)

Step 2 Hs is a measure. By (5), Hδs​(A)≤∑j=1∞​Hs(Aj​). Letting δ→0, we obtain Hs(A)≤j∑​Hs(Aj​).

Step 3 Hs is a Borel measure. By Caratheodory’s criterion (see Theorem 3.14), it suffices to show that if dist(A,B)>0, then Hs(A∪B)=Hs(A)+Hs(B).Let δ<41​dist(A,B). Take a δ-covering {Cj​} of A∪B. Then j=1∑∞​(diamCj​)s≥Cj​∩A=∅∑​(diam(Cj​)s)+Cj​∩B=∅∑​(diam(Cj​)s)≥Hδs​(A)+Hδs​(B).Taking infimum and letting δ→0, we have Hs(A∪B)≥Hs(A)+Hs(B). Furthermore, Hs(A∪B)=Hs(A)+Hs(B) since Hs is a measure.

Step 4 Hs is Borel regular. Fix A⊂Rn. It suffices to show that there exists a Borel set B⊃A such that Hs(A)=Hs(B). WLOG Hs(A)<∞. By definition, there exists a k−1-covering {Cjk​} of A such that j=1∑∞​(diamCjk​)s≤Hs(A)+k−1.As diamC=diamCˉ, we may assume that Cjk​ are closed. Let B:=⋂k=1∞​⋃j=1∞​Cjk​, then B is a Borel set containing A, and Hk−1s​(B)≤Hs(A)+k−1.Letting k→∞, we have Hs(B)=Hs(A).

□

定理 4.6.

(i)

For 0≤s<n, Hs is not locally finite. In particular, Hs is not a Radon measure.

(ii)

Let A⊂Rn be Hs-measurable, and Hs(A)<∞. Then Hs∣A​ is a Radon measure.

(iii)

Hn on Rn is a Radon measure.

(iv)

For all s>n, Hs≡0 on Rn.

证明.

(i)

Let B:={x∈Rn:∣x∣≤1}. It suffices to show that Hs(B)=∞ for 0≤s<n. To cover B using balls of radius δ, we need at least Cn​δ−n such balls. This yields Hδs​(B)≥Cs,n​δ−nδsLetting δ→0, we obtain Hs(B)=∞ since s<n.

(ii)

Apply Theorem 4.5 and Theorem .

(iii)

It suffices to show that Hn(B)<∞. For any δ>0, we can find Cn​δ−n balls of radius δ to cover B, then Hδn​(B)≤Cn′​This implies Hn(B)≤Cn′​<∞.

(iv)

Obvious.

□

定义 4.8. A Borel regular measure μ on a metric space X is called uniformly distributed if 0<μ(B(x,r))=μ(B(y,r))<∞,∀x,y∈X,0<r<∞.

定理 4.9. Let μ and ν be uniformly distributed Radon measures on Rn. Then there exists a constant C such that μ=cν.

证明. Since μ and ν are Radon measures, it suffices to show that μ(U)=cν(U) for all open sets U. Since μ and ν are uniformly distributed, for r>0 define g(r):=μ(B(x,r)),h(r):=ν(B(x,r))Clearly, r→0lim​h(r)ν(U∩B(x,r))​=1,∀x∈UBy Fatou’s lemma, μ(U)​=∫U​r→0lim​h(r)ν(U∩B(x,r))​dμ(x)≤r→0liminf​h(r)1​∫U​ν(U∩B(x,r))dμ(x)=r→0liminf​h(r)1​∫U​μ(U∩B(y,r))dν(y)≤ν(U)r→0liminf​h(r)g(r)​​Similarly, ν(U)≤μ(U)r→0liminf​g(r)h(r)​From the last two estimates, r→0lim​h(r)g(r)​=ν(U)μ(U)​,∀ open UDenote the left-hand side by C, and the proof is complete.

□

Hausdorff Dimension

定理 4.10. Let 0≤s<t<∞ and A⊂Rn.

(i)

If Hs(A)<∞, then Ht(A)=0.

(ii)

If Ht(A)>0, then Hs(A)=∞.

证明.

(i)

By definition, there exists δ>0 and a δ-covering {Cj​} such that j∑​diam(Cj​)s≤Hδs​(A)≤Hs(A)+1As a result, Hδt​(A)​≤j∑​diam(Cj​)t≤δt−sj∑​(diamCj​)s≤δt−s(Hs(A)+1)​Letting δ→0, we have Ht(A)=0.

(ii)

Is equivalent to (i).

□

定义 4.11. The Hausdorff dimension of a set A⊂Rn is dimA​:=sup{s:Hs(A)>0}:=sup{s:Hs(A)=∞}:=inf{t:Ht(A)=0}:=inf{t:Ht(A)<∞}​By Theorem 4.10, this is well-defined.

命题 4.14.

(i)

If A⊂B⊂Rn, then dimA≤dimB.

(ii)

If Ai​⊂Rn,i=1,2,…, then dim(⋃i=1∞​Ai​)=supi​dimAi​.
